body:
Historical and religious foundations

Manipuri is a classical dance tradition originating in Manipur. Its historical foundations include indigenous religious rituals, community festivals and later Vaishnava devotional traditions.

Lai Haraoba is an important indigenous ritual festival of the Meitei community. Its songs, dances and ritual performances preserve traditional accounts of creation and community life. These traditions form part of the wider cultural background from which Manipuri dance developed.

The spread of Vaishnavism enriched Manipuri performance traditions with narratives about Radha and Krishna. Indigenous artistic elements continued to influence the regional character of the dance.

Ras Lila and royal patronage

The classical Ras Lila traditions of Manipur are especially associated with Maharaja Bhagyachandra, an 18th-century ruler who contributed to their organization and development.

Ras Lila depicts the devotional relationship between Radha, Krishna and the Gopis. Graceful, continuous movement and restrained facial expression help convey spiritual devotion and emotional tenderness.

Commonly identified Ras traditions include Maha Ras, Vasanta Ras and Kunja Ras. Manipuri dance also presents Bala Lila, which depicts episodes associated with the childhood of Krishna.

Costume and visual identity

The characteristic female Ras costume is called Potloi or Patloi. It includes a rigid cylindrical skirt known as Kumin or Kumil, decorated with embroidery and reflective ornaments. A transparent veil, blouse and decorative head ornaments complete the costume.

The cylindrical shape distinguishes the Manipuri Ras costume from the pleated front fan of Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi.

Music, Pung Cholom and Sankirtana

The music accompanying Manipuri performances has a strong devotional character. The Pung is a traditional Manipuri drum, while Kartal refers to cymbals used in devotional music.

Pung Cholom is a vigorous performance tradition in which dancers play the Pung while executing rhythmic movements. It demonstrates that Manipuri performing traditions include energetic forms as well as the gentle movement associated with Ras Lila.

Sankirtana of Manipur is a ritual tradition combining devotional singing, drumming and dancing. It is performed in religious and social settings and is closely connected to Manipuri Vaishnava culture.

UNESCO inscribed Sankirtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur, on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. This inscription concerns the specified Sankirtana tradition, not the entirety of Manipuri classical dance. Its inscription remained listed as of 25 November 2026.

Major exponents and institutional preservation

ExponentAssociation
Guru Bipin SinghPreservation, teaching and popularization of Manipuri dance
Nayana JhaveriManipuri performance and teaching outside Manipur
Darshana JhaveriManipuri performance, research and institutional development
Rajkumar Singhajit SinghProminent Manipuri dancer and choreographer

The Jhaveri sisters trained under Guru Bipin Singh and contributed significantly to the spread of Manipuri dance outside its region of origin. Darshana Jhaveri also helped establish Manipuri Nartanalaya.

The Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy in Imphal traces its establishment to 1954 and functions under the Sangeet Natak Akademi. It is an important centre for teaching and preserving the dance and music traditions of Manipur.

Prelims focus

  • Manipuri developed from indigenous ritual and Vaishnava devotional traditions.
  • Maharaja Bhagyachandra is associated with the development of Ras Lila.
  • Potloi and its cylindrical Kumin skirt are characteristic of female Ras dancers.
  • Pung Cholom combines drumming and vigorous dancing.
  • Guru Bipin Singh and the Jhaveri sisters are associated with Manipuri.
  • UNESCO inscribed Manipur's Sankirtana tradition in 2013.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 13; CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 11–12; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Nayana Jhaveri award citation, 1977, and Darshana Jhaveri award citation, 1996; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy institutional history; UNESCO, Sankirtana, Ritual Singing, Drumming and Dancing of Manipur, 2013 inscription. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Origin and religious background

Sattriya is a classical dance tradition originating in Assam. It developed within the Neo-Vaishnava religious movement led by the saint, poet and reformer Srimanta Sankaradeva during the 15th and 16th centuries.

Sankaradeva used music, dance, drama and congregational worship to communicate devotional teachings. His religious movement emphasized devotion to one supreme deity, particularly through worship centred on Krishna, and is commonly known as Ekasarana Nama Dharma.

His disciple Madhavadeva contributed significantly to the continuation and development of the religious and artistic traditions.

Sattras as centres of preservation

The name Sattriya is derived from Sattra, a Vaishnava monastic institution of Assam. Sattras served as centres of religious worship, education and artistic training.

For centuries, resident male devotees and monks preserved Sattriya through devotional performances and religious festivals. Majuli, the river island region of Assam, is particularly associated with important sattra traditions.

As Sattriya developed beyond its monastic setting, it became a public stage tradition performed by both women and men.

Dance, drama and devotional literature

Sattriya cannot be understood solely as an isolated dance tradition because its historical development is closely connected with religious music and drama.

TermMeaning
Ankiya NatTraditional one-act devotional plays associated with Sankaradeva
BhaonaThe performance tradition presenting such religious dramas
BorgeetDevotional musical compositions associated with Sankaradeva and Madhavadeva
Gayan-BayanA tradition involving singers, instrumentalists and rhythmic performance
NamgharA congregational prayer hall associated with Assamese Vaishnava worship

The Sattriya repertoire includes devotional and dramatic items, as well as independent dance compositions. Its religious narratives commonly draw upon Vaishnava literature and episodes concerning Krishna.

Music and costume

Borgeet compositions are an important source of musical accompaniment in Sattriya. These devotional songs are organized within established melodic traditions.

The characteristic accompanying instruments include the Khol, a double-headed drum, and Tal, or metallic cymbals. The flute and other instruments may also accompany performances.

Sattriya costumes reflect Assamese textile traditions. Locally woven silk garments, including traditional Assamese silk varieties, are commonly used with regional jewellery. White and cream garments with gold-coloured ornamentation are particularly associated with several traditional presentations.

National recognition and preservation

The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognized Sattriya as a classical dance form in 2000. It is the most recently included form among the conventional list of 8 principal Indian classical dances.

The date of recognition must be distinguished from the origin of the dance. Sattriya had already existed for centuries within Assam's Vaishnava institutions before receiving this recognition.

The Sattriya Kendra of the Sangeet Natak Akademi in Guwahati supports documentation, training and promotion of the tradition. Important exponents include Rasheswar Saikia Barbayan, Jatin Goswami and Indira P. P. Bora.

Prelims focus

  • Sattriya originates in Assam.
  • Its development is traditionally associated with Srimanta Sankaradeva and his Neo-Vaishnava movement.
  • Sattras are Vaishnava monastic institutions; Namghars are congregational prayer halls.
  • Ankiya Nat, Bhaona and Borgeet are associated traditions.
  • Khol is a characteristic percussion instrument.
  • Trap: The year 2000 refers to classical recognition, not the creation of Sattriya.

[References: CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 14–15; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Cultural Packages, Sattriya Dance; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Sattriya Kendra institutional information; Sangeet Sattra, About Sangeet Sattra; Sattriya Dance Company, history and classical recognition of Sattriya. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Institutional preservation in independent India

Classical dance has traditionally been transmitted through teachers, hereditary artistic communities and the Guru-Shishya tradition. Modern institutions supplement these methods through organized training, research, documentation, scholarships, festivals and public performances.

Sangeet Natak Akademi

The Sangeet Natak Akademi is India's national academy for music, dance and drama. It was established through a Government of India resolution in 1952 and formally inaugurated on 28 January 1953 by President Rajendra Prasad.

Headquartered in New Delhi, it functions as an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Culture. Its responsibilities include the promotion, preservation, documentation and recognition of India's performing arts.

It supports institutions specializing in particular performing arts, organizes cultural programmes and confers awards recognizing artistic contributions.

Important dance institutions

InstitutionLocationPrincipal association
KalakshetraChennai, Tamil NaduBharatanatyam and related arts
Kerala KalamandalamCheruthuruthy, KeralaKathakali, Mohiniyattam and Kerala performing arts
Kathak KendraNew DelhiKathak
Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance AcademyImphal, ManipurManipuri
Sattriya KendraGuwahati, AssamSattriya

The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training also contributes to cultural education through training programmes and educational resources on India's artistic heritage.

Gujarat's contribution to classical dance

Although none of the conventional 8 principal classical dance forms originated exclusively in Gujarat, the state has made important contributions to their preservation, teaching and modern development. Ahmedabad and Vadodara are particularly important centres.

Mrinalini Sarabhai and Darpana Academy

Mrinalini Sarabhai received training in Bharatanatyam and Kathakali and became a major contributor to India's modern classical dance movement.

She established Darpana Academy of Performing Arts in Ahmedabad together with Vikram Sarabhai. The academy has promoted dance, music, theatre and other performing arts through teaching and public performances.

Her daughter Mallika Sarabhai is also a prominent exponent of Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi and is associated with Darpana.

Kumudini Lakhia and Kadamb

Kumudini Lakhia was a distinguished Kathak exponent whose work helped expand the possibilities of group choreography and contemporary presentation within the classical tradition.

She started Kadamb Dance Centre in Ahmedabad in 1964. Kadamb became an important institution for Kathak training, choreography and performance.

Her national civilian honours included the Padma Shri in 1987, Padma Bhushan in 2010 and Padma Vibhushan in 2025, conferred posthumously.

Darpana is associated particularly with Mrinalini Sarabhai and Bharatanatyam, while Kadamb is associated with Kumudini Lakhia and Kathak. Both institutions are located in Ahmedabad.

The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda

The Faculty of Performing Arts of the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda in Vadodara provides university-level education in performing arts. Its Department of Dance includes training in Kathak and Bharatanatyam.

The institution traces its historical foundations to the music school established under Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III in 1886, reflecting the long tradition of royal support for artistic education in Baroda.

Modhera Dance Festival

The Modhera Dance Festival, also known as Uttarardh Mahotsav, is associated with the Sun Temple at Modhera in Mehsana district.

The Solanki-period temple provides a historic architectural setting for performances by artists representing different Indian dance traditions. The festival is traditionally associated with January, following Uttarayan.

The festival demonstrates how Gujarat's architectural heritage can support the preservation and public presentation of living performing arts. It is a cultural platform rather than a separate classical dance form.

Prelims focus

  • Sangeet Natak Akademi: established by resolution in 1952 and inaugurated in 1953.
  • Kalakshetra: Chennai; Kerala Kalamandalam: Cheruthuruthy.
  • Darpana Academy: Mrinalini Sarabhai, Ahmedabad.
  • Kadamb: Kumudini Lakhia, Ahmedabad, started in 1964.
  • Faculty of Performing Arts, Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda: Vadodara.
  • Uttarardh Mahotsav: Sun Temple, Modhera, Mehsana district.

[References: Sangeet Natak Akademi, About the Akademi and constituent institution profiles; Kalakshetra Foundation, institutional history; Indian Council for Cultural Relations, Darpana Academy — Mrinalini Sarabhai, 2019 empanelment record; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Natarani Amphitheatre institutional information; Government of India, Padma Vibhushan citation for Kumudini Lakhia, 2025; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Faculty of Performing Arts, About Faculty; Gujarat Tourism, Modhera Dance Festival. Institutional information consulted 25 November 2026; the festival period is its traditional timing, not a confirmed future event schedule.]
